name: DeckCraft
tagline: A native slide editor with PPTX import and export, animations, and both web and desktop apps.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: If what you actually want is a way to write slides and present them, an agent can hand you a working deck tool in an afternoon: markdown in, keyboard-driven presenting, PDF out. What it cannot hand you in one session is a real WYSIWYG canvas with snapping, grouping, z-order, text boxes that behave, and an animation timeline. PPTX is the other wall: reading and writing OOXML well enough that a coworker opening your file in PowerPoint sees what you saw is a months-long fidelity grind, not a feature. So the honest split is that the personal use case is cheap and the interop use case is not. Build the markdown deck tool, keep something else around for the one time a year someone demands a .pptx.
coreLoopDIY: Turns markdown files into a presentable deck in the browser with speaker notes, a presenter view, and PDF export.
requirements: Chromium installed if you want automated PDF export
whatYouLose: Direct manipulation editing: dragging, snapping, grouping, precise positioning
PPTX import and export, which is where most real-world slide pain lives
Animation and transition authoring beyond basic fragment reveals
A desktop app and offline-first file handling
Templates and theming that look designed rather than defaulted
moatNotes: Format fidelity is the unglamorous part. Anyone can render slides; matching what PowerPoint does with a grouped shape containing rotated text is the actual product.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because slides are rarely a solo artifact. The moment a deck has to be handed to someone who will open it in PowerPoint or Keynote, you are buying file format fidelity, and that is a thing people reasonably pay for rather than debug. On top of that, editing slides is a direct-manipulation task, and the gap between a competent WYSIWYG canvas and a homemade one is obvious within about four seconds of use. If your decks never leave your laptop, none of this applies to you.
notes: The presenting part is a weekend; the editing canvas is a career. Fine if your slides never need to open in PowerPoint.
prompt:
Build a local-first markdown presentation tool. Empty folder, no backend, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: Vite + TypeScript + Reveal.js. No React, no component library, no database.

Structure:
- /decks/*.md are the source of truth. One file per deck.
- Slides split on a line containing only ---, vertical sub-slides on only --.
- YAML frontmatter per deck: title, theme, author, date.
- Speaker notes: anything after a line containing only Note: in a slide.

Build these:
1. A dev server that lists all decks in /decks at the index route with title and slide count.
2. A deck route that renders the markdown through Reveal.js markdown plugin, with syntax highlighting for code fences and KaTeX for $...$ math.
3. Hot reload: editing a .md file re-renders the open deck without losing the current slide index.
4. Presenter view in a second window: current slide, next slide, speaker notes, elapsed timer, keyboard-synced to the main window via BroadcastChannel.
5. Three themes as plain CSS files in /themes, selected by frontmatter. Dark, light, and one high-contrast. Make the type scale actually readable at the back of a room: body text no smaller than 28px equivalent.
6. Images referenced relatively from /decks/assets resolve correctly in dev and build.
7. npm run export DECK=name produces a PDF via Playwright driving Reveal's print-pdf mode, written to /out.
8. npm run build emits a static self-contained folder per deck that can be opened from the filesystem.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: PPTX import or export, drag-and-drop WYSIWYG editing, animation timelines, real-time collaboration, cloud sync, auth.

Secrets: none needed. If you add anything optional, read it from .env and commit .env.example only.

Ship a README with three example decks in /decks, one per theme, and the exact commands to run, present, and export.
